item.title: Rematriated latte stone symbolizes resilience, identity, renewal

item.content:encoded:
Members of the Marianas High School Polksai Guma Chamorro Club performed traditional chants Wednesday morning during a rematriation ceremony at the NMI Museum of History & Culture, where cultural leaders welcomed home an ancient Åtchu’ Latti’ returned to the Marianas after more than a century.

The Northern Marianas Humanities Council and the museum hosted the event, marking the return of the latte stone originally taken from Rota in the early 20th century and held for decades in the Bishop Museum’s Hornbostel Collection.

The ceremony also included the signing of a proclamation designating October 2026 as CNMI Humanities Month.

Humanities Council Executive Director Leo Pangelinan said the homecoming reflects the community’s resilience and commitment to cultural stewardship, especially after recent storms and economic strain.

He tied the event to this year’s Humanities Month theme, Rooted in Heritage, Seeded to Flourish, noting that “resilience is knowing what sustains us.”

Lt. Gov. Dennis Mendiola signed the proclamation and urged families to preserve language, stories, and traditions for younger generations. He said the humanities live not only in institutions but in everyday cultural practice.

NMI Museum acting Board Chair Mona Mercado described the rematriation as “a return of spirit, memory, and belonging,” recounting the latte stone’s journey from Rota to Hawaii and its rediscovery by Saipan residents Martin and Linda Naputi. She said the museum will temporarily house the stone until its original site on Rota is identified.

Museum officials said the latte’s return was made possible through collaboration with the CNMI Historic Preservation Office, Bishop Museum, Guam Museum, Chamorro Affairs Office and the Guam Cultural Repository.

item.title: Juan Ogo Blaz’s Medal of Honor nomination awaits president’s signature

item.content:encoded:
The nomination to award the late Sgt. Maj. Juan Ogo Blaz the Medal of Honor has reached its final step, nearly 58 years after his actions during the Vietnam War.

Del. James Moylan announced the status during a press conference Wednesday, saying the nomination now awaits President Donald Trump’s signature. If approved, Blaz would become the first CHamoru service member from Guam to receive the nation’s highest military decoration for valor.

Moylan was joined by Blaz’s daughters Darlene and Dionisia “Marylou” Blaz, Vice Speaker Tony Ada, Sen. Sabrina Salas Matanane, and Guam veterans.

On Jan. 18, 1969, Blaz was serving as a staff sergeant with the 82nd Airborne Division in Vietnam when his platoon leader was wounded. Blaz assumed command, helped evacuate injured soldiers, and led an assault against enemy positions.

Despite being wounded twice under enemy fire, he refused evacuation, and exposed himself to enemy fire to mark enemy positions for airstrikes. He accepted medical treatment only after those positions were neutralized.

In 1994 , Blaz received the Distinguished Service Cross for his actions. The current effort seeks to upgrade that award to the Medal of Honor.

Moylan said he worked alongside retired Col. Danny Santos during his first year in Congress to advance Blaz’s case. During the 118th Congress, Moylan pursued legislation through the fiscal year 2025 National Defense Authorization Act to support reconsideration of the nomination. He also raised the case with military leadership and helped gather bipartisan support from members of Congress urging the president to approve the award.

Santos has helped gather testimony and documentation to support the effort. He has also worked to seek Medal of Honor upgrades for two other Guam Army veterans, Martin Manglona and Joseph Manuel Perez, whose Distinguished Service Crosses he said should be reconsidered.

During the press conference, Santos said the recognition would honor Blaz’s sacrifice.

“It’s this honor that is finally bestowed upon him. Truly, an honor of recognition for his sacrifice, for himself, for his platoon. Most importantly, to show the people of Guam that we continuously fight for what we truly deserve,” Santos said.

Moylan said his office will continue following up on the nomination. No date has been announced for a potential ceremony. The family is expected to receive notifications as plans develop.

If approved, Blaz’s Medal of Honor would mark a historic recognition as the first CHamoru recipient of the Medal of Honor.

item.title: Guam, CNMI residents advised to get ready for possible rough weather this weekend
item.description: Forecasters are looking at the potential passage of a tropical storm or typhoon this weekend anywhere from south of Guam to the Northern Islands. While the exact timing, location and intensity of the storm are uncertain, emergency managers are advising residents of Guam and the Northern Marianas to begin making early preparations.
item.content:encoded:
Forecasters are looking at the potential passage of a tropical storm or typhoon this weekend anywhere from south of Guam to the Northern Islands.

While the exact timing, location and intensity of the storm are uncertain, emergency managers are advising residents of Guam and the Northern Marianas to begin making early preparations.

On Tuesday, Invest 96W was 200 miles west of Kosrae and about 1,300 miles east-southeast of Guam. It was expected to move west-northwest and could pass near the islands Saturday and into Sunday.

National Weather Service Guam says the system could reach at least tropical storm strength and possibly typhoon strength.

No watches or warnings are in effect yet, but heavy rain, gusty winds and hazardous seas are possible.

Residents can prepare by cleaning their storm drains, trimming overgrown vegetation and calling authorities about overgrown vegetation near power and utility lines.

Households should also check and restock emergency kits with at least seven days of drinking water, non-perishable food, medications and supplies.

item.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico prevail against White House — for now

item.content:encoded:
A federal judge ruled late Tuesday that President Trump cannot ban news organizations from covering him at the White House because he does not like the nature of their coverage - at least, not until the matter goes to a formal trial.

U.S. District Court Judge Timothy J. Kelly found that Trump's decision to bar more than 70 journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico violated their fundamental free speech in two separate ways as well as their due process rights. Both rights are enshrined in the Bill of Rights to the U.S. Constitution.

The news organizations sued last month after the Trump administration denied them access. The judge granted a temporary restraining order to CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Sept. 24.

Kelly pointed repeatedly to Trump's own public statements and social media posts to construct his conclusion that Trump was not responding to national security concerns. Instead, he wrote, Trump sought to pressure news outlets to cover him more favorably by stripping them of press credentials to gain access to the White House.

"President Trump's own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before," Kelly wrote in the opinion.

He later continued, "[T]he ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs' access to the White House press area -- a space open to many of their competitors -- thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials."

Theodore J. Boutrous, the noted First Amendment attorney representing the three U.S. news outlets, had argued in court last week that Trump was the best witness his clients could offer for their case - because the president was so blatant about not liking the tenor of their coverage. Late Tuesday, after the release of Kelly's ruling, he hailed the judge's words.

"When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said in a statement shared with NPR.

"Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn't like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers," Boutrous wrote. "The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound."

The White House did not immediately return NPR's requests for comment. Nor did the president speak publicly about the ruling in the first hours after the ruling was released.

Kelly, a Trump appointee, turned aside the U.S. Justice Department's arguments invoking national security concerns and the objections the White House took with their reporting. Trump has said coverage is framed in a way to drag him down and make his Democratic critics look good.

The judge also rejected the department's claims that the court should not weigh in on such matters. Kelly had ruled against the Trump administration during the president's first term in office on a related matter involving efforts to bar then CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta. And Kelly pointed to other precedents that he said must guide his conclusions, even as the Justice Department argued in court they were wrongly decided.

Even so, Kelly took pains to note that he did not utterly dismiss those as valid governmental concerns.

"No one should interpret the Court's decision to suggest that President Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded," Kelly wrote, "or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed."

Even so, Kelly found that the White House's actions to put the president's words into practice had caused a kind of irreparable harm. Trump was not required to admit the reporters to the White House. Once they were credentialed to do so, under earlier court rulings, those credentials could not be stripped away simply because the president or other administration officials do not like their coverage.

The Justice Department invoked national security only in court filings days after the White House acted against the reporters. And the news outlets were neither given fair warning of what was ahead nor a means to object ahead of time. The White House communications office sent letters expressing concern over accuracy and what it said were national security disclosures days later and gave the journalists several days to respond and appeal.

Kelly wrote that the Justice Department's presentation was inadequate to make a compelling case. And he said that after-the-fact notification did not constitute an adequate process to be warned about consequences and to appeal the punishment.

"It is not hard to conclude that President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him," Kelly wrote. And that, he wrote, represents a form of unlawful retaliation.

The ruling did not, however, address the question of the administration's periodic refusal since the ban to permit CNN's journalists into smaller spaces where the full press corps cannot fit simultaneously, such as Air Force One or the Oval Office.

That has made it impossible for CNN to serve as the designated representative of the video pool.

The pool - made up of CNN and four competitors (ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC) - share costs and logistical obligations to capture video of Trump at every public appearance, even in tightly held locations.

Even after Kelly earlier issued a temporary restraining order compelling the administration to allow the reporters back into the White House, the order was observed unevenly. CNN was periodically blocked by the administration from representing the pool either generally or in tight spaces. In one recent instance, CNN was blocked from accompanying Trump aboard Air Force One on a trip to Tennessee.

The three major U.S. news organizations sued shortly after reporters for the outlets reported their credentials, which give them daily access to the White House, were confiscated.

The administration has waged a multi-front battle against the press, including an early review of the broadcast licenses for ABC's local TV stations that could lead to them being revoked. It also forced news outlets out from the Pentagon when they did not agree to withhold any reports that had not been authorized for release ahead of time. The administration has launched investigations of all major networks — including NPR — except Fox, which is controlled by Rupert Murdoch, the president's ally, and successfully pressured the Republican leaders of Congress to pull back all federal funds for public media.

Last week, the Department of Justice said it was investigating five major television networks - CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News, alleging that they have broken antitrust laws when they decided to stick together after the president banned CNN.

As a private citizen, Trump has sued the New York Times , CNN, the Des Moines Register, the BBC, and Wall Street Journal (also owned by Murdoch). ABC settled a Trump lawsuit ahead of his return to office and CBS settled days before its corporate owner received the green light from Trump's pick as the nation's chief broadcast regulator to sell itself to its new owners, allies of the president.

item.content:encoded:
Pope Leo XIV had surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerous growth in his lung, the Vatican announced.

The surgery, performed at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, involved removing the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung, according to a statement by Leo's doctors released by the church. Lung tissue examined after the surgery confirmed a previous test that revealed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said.

Adenocarcinoma of the lung is the most common form of lung cancer in the United States, representing about 40% of all lung cancers, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.

The Pope's surgery, which the doctors said was successful, lasted about 90 minutes, after which Leo awoke normally and, following a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the hospital's 10th floor.

At 71 years old, Leo is relatively young for a pope – and remains physically active. He works out weekly, including regular tennis matches with his personal secretary and enjoys riding horses at Castel Gandolfo, the papal retreat.

Leo has not been known to smoke, but there is a history of cancer in the pope's family. On Tuesday, the Vatican announced that Leo's older brother Louis, who lives in Florida, is currently hospitalized with a form of cancer. And Leo's mother, Mildred, died of cancer in 1990 at age 77. Back in 1984, while living in Rome, the future pope wrote to several friends saying, "my mother continues to undergo chemotherapy treatments. … She's a tough lady and handles it all well, which makes it a little easier for me being so far from Chicago."

The Vatican says the Pope has essentially cleared his public schedule for the next several days, until at least October 20. The Vatican has yet to announce any further treatments.

item.title: Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal
item.description: A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to rescind his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine." item.content:encoded:
A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to rescind his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine."

Last week, Trump announced via social media he had struck a deal with Putin, whereby Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter."

"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump wrote.

His announcement stunned lawmakers, who passed legislation this summer directing the president to impose significant tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil.

Those sanctions are aimed at targeting Russian officials, companies and financial institutions helping fuel Russia's war in Ukraine. The legislation was named in memory of the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham , who helped negotiate Trump's support for the package.

"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded," wrote six Republican and six Democratic senators in a letter Tuesday to the president.

"The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9 th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," it read.

Senators said they recognized the need to lower energy costs for Americans — but maintained that allowing Russian diesel into global markets will offer "limited to no relief to Americans."

They added the deal "only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."

When asked about the letter, the White House referred back to comments President Trump made to reporters on Tuesday about concerns that Russia will use proceeds from the diesel agreement to purchase weapons.

"Nobody's telling me anything," Trump said. "That's a diesel deal. Not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices."

The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse. They were joined by Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.

item.title: A judge blocks the government's tree-clearing spree at a municipal D.C. golf course
item.description: A federal judge has temporarily barred the Trump administration from cutting down additional trees at a D.C. municipal golf course, the latest example of a court intervening in the government's efforts to reshape pieces of the nation's capital. The long-simmering fight over East Potomac Golf Links — which President Trump wants to redevelop into a championship-level course — erupted over the weeken
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge has temporarily barred the Trump administration from cutting down additional trees at a D.C. municipal golf course, the latest example of a court intervening in the government's efforts to reshape pieces of the nation's capital.

The long-simmering fight over East Potomac Golf Links — which President Trump wants to redevelop into a championship-level course — erupted over the weekend, after the administration cut down hundreds of trees with little notice.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes had ordered the administration in May to get court approval before cutting down more than 10 trees at the golf course. Officials notified the court just before 5 p.m. on Friday of their plan to remove "up to 529 trees" in phases starting on Saturday — and had razed at least 430 by the end of the day, prompting Reyes to call an emergency hearing on Monday.

"What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility with me in this case," Reyes said during the nearly four-hour hearing, held via videoconference.

Reyes ordered a short-term stop to the tree-clearings, which she extended on Tuesday through Oct. 26. She warned Monday that "if that order is violated by two seconds, there are going to be contempt proceedings."

Reyes also ordered top officials from the Department of Interior and the National Park Service to testify at a hearing next Monday, to shed more light on the government's motivations and the future of the historic course.

"The questions go to whether or not I've been lied to," Reyes said. "Whether I've been lied to in declarations about the plans, whether or not I've been lied to about the timing of things, and whether I've been lied to about what kind of notice the court was going to receive."

East Potomac has emerged as another flashpoint in Trump's unilateral quest to remake D.C ., and it's the subject of a lawsuit by critics who fear it could go the way of the now-lost White House East Wing unless a court intervenes. The D.C. Preservation League, along with two concerned residents, sued the government in February over what it calls an unlawful takeover.

"This is a tactic we're seen before from the Trump-Vance administration – act quickly to irrevocably alter a cherished national landmark, just to advance another one of President Trump's pet vanity projects," Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward — one of the firms involved in the lawsuit — said in a statement this weekend.

Perryman told NPR on Tuesday that the golf course is the latest in a pattern of the Trump administration "undermining the entire checks and balances process in this country, which includes undermining court proceedings."

Trump has long floated the idea of redeveloping East Potomac into a championship-caliber course and announced plans to do so earlier this year, though his target Sept. 1 start date has come and gone without a formal proposal.

The prospect — and the lack of clarity since — has raised alarm among locals concerned about losing access to the historically affordable course and to the surrounding recreational area, which is popular with cyclists, runners, fishers and picnickers.

"This is a broader story than just about golf, especially when there's been this little transparency, … to say, 'Here's what the future of this little man-made peninsula is actually going to look like,'" Alex Rosen, a D.C.-based consultant who started the nonprofit Save East Po, told NPR in July.

A National Park Service official said in a Friday court filing that plans for renovations "remain in the conceptual stage." And the Interior Department told NPR in a statement on Tuesday that it is "committed to continuing the relationships we have built with the local golf communities to ensure these courses are safe, beautiful, open, affordable, enjoyable, accessible, and world-class."

But critics are growing increasingly concerned about the process itself. They worry the Trump administration is using so-called routine maintenance as a pretext to begin redevelopment without the proper authorization.

"You can't continuously say, 'There's no plan' … while you're clearly taking steps to effect a plan," Rosen, who is not involved in the lawsuit, told NPR after watching the hearing. "It's just frankly lying."

At Monday's hearing, Reyes expressed regret that she hadn't issued a formal restraining order earlier, which she said was because "I have done everything humanly possible to give the government the benefit of the doubt in this case."

For example, after the administration quietly removed what it has since said were roughly 150 dying and invasive trees in late August, Reyes acknowledged that people were upset but declined to intervene: "I am not the Lorax ," she said at an early September hearing.

By Monday, that benefit of the doubt was gone. When a government lawyer said they had done their best to notify the court, Reyes offered a sharp rebuke.

"You did not do your best," she said, voice raised. "You did your absolute worst."

Perryman, of Democracy Forward, said, "What was really remarkable about the hearing yesterday is that the government did not appear to have a defense for its failure to notify the court."

In Friday's court filing, National Mall and Memorial Parks Superintendent Kevin Griess described the tree-clearing as part of an effort "to address deferred maintenance needs and implement treatment recommendations to restore the cultural landscape."

Griess specifically cited a 2019 National Park Service report about D.C. municipal golf courses, which says several waves of tree planting at East Potomac over the last century have obscured views and changed the feel of the course from its original 1920s "links-style" design.

Griess said in his filing that NPS was able to act on the report because it had received a temporary surge of "approximately 20 to 50 trained personnel capable of performing labor-intensive grounds maintenance activities." Under questioning in court, he confirmed that surge was connected to the administration's 250th anniversary events, including the IndyCar race on the National Mall in August.

But critics are skeptical, given the president's public statements. Alex Dickson, one of the plaintiffs, said in a statement that "the administration is using a preservation report as cover to begin tearing out the course it was written to save."

Griess said he had gotten the green light last week from Frank Lands, the park service's deputy director of operations. At the judge's request, Lands then joined the hearing from his car in a parking lot. He said he had gotten the directive from Greg Wischer, deputy chief of staff to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

Wischer was not reachable to join the hearing, despite Reyes' request that he do so. She has ordered Wischer and Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, to testify at another hearing next Monday.

The Interior Department didn't answer NPR's questions about the timeline and resources for the tree-clearing, but said in a statement that "President Donald J. Trump is fulfilling his commitment to make D.C. Safe and Beautiful as shown by the working fountains, clean parks and safe streets across the district for the first time in decades."

In granting the plaintiffs' request for an extended restraining order on Tuesday, Reyes wrote that they had "proven they will likely suffer irreparable harm absent injunctive relief." She also said the government must provide "three business days' written advance notice prior to making any irreparable modification" to the golf course.
